posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I would like to pose a question concerning reference beams. I guess the standard reference beam in holography is from a spatial filter, but I've often wondered how much spatial coherence is needed. 

Say for example, we bounce a laser beam off an aspirin tablet. The beam will be about 2mm in diameter, and the resulting reflected beam will be highly diverging. I tried this, and the spread beam is quite clean. Due the high divergence of the beam, the aspirin tablet will be quite close to the hologram, say 10cm (4 inches). I am wondering if this will work for a reference beam.

posts.author: Steven
posts.content_md:
Seasons greetings Joe,

I think you will find that the Aspirin tablet will depolarize your ref beam.

Do a check using polarized sun glasses.

I don't use a spatial filter when shooting DCG.

I'm using a 9.5mm focal length concave mirror to expand my ref beam.

I do have to hunt around to find a reasonable clean spot on the mirror, it's not perfect.

I can't see a noticeable effect in the finished hologram.

The only way to see if you need spatial filtering (for display holography) is to project the expanding ref beam onto a white screen/large piece of paper and look at it. I look for a reasonably smooth area of even illumination without bulls eyes, or other artefacts.

I think that very short focal length objectives produce poor quality ref beams if not using a spatial filter, unless you find a clean spot that may be off axis.

Steven.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Hi Steven,

Happy Holidays

Yes, I'm certain the beam will be depolarized. But, in my early days I used a randomly-polarized laser, and was able to get good results. So maybe the polarization problem can be worked around. Also, since the point-source of the reference beam will be so close to the center of the plate (about 3 to 4 inches), only one of the rays from the beam can be made to strike the plate at Brewster's angle (say for example the center ray). The others will veer off of Brewster's angle, more so as they reach the edge of the plate.

I've found an improvement over the aspirin tablet, which is a modified piece of flashed opal. The opal coating was originally about 0.8mm thick, which resulted in high losses. I ground the coating down to maybe around 0.2mm using wet 220 grit. I'm getting about 16% transmittance with a clean beam spread, which isn't bad, since I was only getting about 33% when using a 100x objective, with no pinhole.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks Steven.

The effort to reduce distortions in the replay is one-half of the walnut. It will also solve another problem, if the reference source is close to the plate. The main question on my mind is how "small" the point-source of the reference beam must be. My usual reference beam has been either a convex lens, or a spatial filter, both of which focus the light to a point, after which it spreads out. The same is true with your concave mirror. I have a similar concave mirror also, which is a good solution to the reference beam problem, in most cases. (Like you said, a reasonably clean spot on the mirror can usually be found.) But to work well in my setup, it would need to have a focal length maybe (?) around 1 or 2mm. I have searched for micro-optics (lenses or mirrors) which are around these dimensions (both diameter and focal length would be pretty similar, I think). But so far the closest thing I've seen is a ball lens, which would definitely still require a pinhole, and this would likely be very difficult to implement (maybe a 2 micron pinhole).

The modified flashed opal is showing promise. Surprisingly, when ground down to ~0.2mm, the transmitted beam shows quite a bit of polarization maintenance. As the opal gets thinner, the amount of transmitted light increases, and the speckle in the spread beam gets more substantial. However, a spatially filtered beam also shows quite a bit of speckle in the spread beam (on objects), and I haven't done a side-by-side comparison yet. Today I checked a spread 532/633 beam using the opal, and it was a beautiful, even, solid yellow color. Far better than anything I've seen with a spatial filter. My only concern is that the raw beam (~2mm) strikes the opal directly, and the beam is then scattered, without being focused to a point. I don't know what effect this will have on the hologram and its reconstruction. My holograms in the past have had a reference beam which had previously been focused to a point.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Being the experimentalist that I am, I would say go ahead and shoot one, what the heck.

I have seen holograms shot (at Lake Forest College Summer Holography Workshops) using the scatter from a ground glass used as the reference beam. But there was a speckle pattern on the final hologram, but that was from the ground glass. I didn’t shoot it, a participant did, and we were surprised that it worked. How well, I can’t say, not having a sample in front of me, but we were amazed that it worked.

However the theoretical side of me is thinking of that over a 2 mm diameter spot it could be imagined there are many point sources, each making their own interference pattern system. Would these overlapping systems “fill in” each others’ fringes (a bright fringe from one falling into another’s dim fringe) so their contrast is lowered, possibly to an unusable level?

This could be proven geometrically, if one had the time to indulge in such fun pastimes. I don’t at the moment. The reason the above experiment worked was that the angular separation between the extreme “reference points” was small, as the ground glass with a similar sized laser spot was about a meter away from the SBR hologram. Your scenario has a much closer spot, and 2 mm is a quite large displacement when we consider the size of the recording waves to be .000532 and .000632 mm!

So why not shoot one and see what happens!

posts.author: unixboy
posts.content_md:
This thread is interesting and inspiring. As Ed Wesly said, the scattering light from the point laser shooting on the ground glass can be used as reference beam but with the problem of speckle noise. I did try this in 2006 using white paper glued to glass rather than ground glass. The diameter of the laser point on the paper surface can be adjusted using a focusing lens. If the diameter of laser beam is small enough, then the speckle noise is significant but good spacial coherence. If the diameter of laser beam is 1-2mm, the appeared "cleanness" of the reflected laser light is good but with poor spacial coherence unless it is used long distance from the hologram plate (such case results in low laser intensity and very long exposure time). The transmission hologram made from such 1-2mm diameter "white-paper-scattering-laser" reference beam shows obscure (bad sharpness) images when viewed with a good spacial coherence laser. However, at that time, I forgot to test the quality of the image viewed with 1-2mm diameter "white-paper-scattering-laser" beam. The hologram is not at hand and I have to make a new one to see the result. I would say it is good sharpness but weak image. Not tested yet.

Actually, for transmission hologram, if we put the processed hologram in the recording configuration, illuminate the object with laser (i.e. you are using the original complicated object beam as a reconstruction beam!), can we see the reconstructed "object" beam of the point laser which was the reference beam? In this case, we swap the object beam and the reference beam. The answer is YES but very weak brightness. This is an easy experiment and everyone in the forum can do this quickly. For the weak brightness of the reconstructed point laser, I still don't quite understand the reason in the point of view of mathematics but will do so. The advantage of experiment is easy to test for what we think but more work of mathematics is needed for understanding the phenomenon.

From my experimental thinking, I would say that the larger of the area of the reference light source (or the larger of the "apparent diameter" of the reference light source), the weaker the brightness of reconstructed image, if the same recording angle, diffraction efficiency were obtained.

Mathematical discussions of non-standard reference beams are welcome. Please.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
The flashed opal is showing a different effect compared to etched glass. Although the white opal coating is much too thick, if it's ground down, the transmission increases. The lack of speckle stays about the same until the thickness is reduced to about 0.3mm (original thickness of opal coating ~0.8mm). The first photo shows the piece of material I have, and some test squares were cut out from this. The second photo shows one of the squares, with a ball lens glued to the front. The ball lens is not really a lens, just a 3mm acrylic sphere. The laser light strikes the opal coating from behind, then the diffused light enters the ball lens, is focused, then spreads out. Surprisingly, there is no additional speckle (or other noise) apparent in the output from the ball lens. The divergence is good (but of course not as good compared to the beam emerging from plain opal. The problem at this point is light loss, which is large.

In another test, I used an air-eraser to etch the back surface of another acrylic ball with 600 grit. No opal was used. The output from the ball had a lot of speckle, and was not acceptable. The output from the opal/ball lens was very nice, like a spatial filter, but very weak. This was just a rough test however. There seems to be some kind of effect with the flashed opal material, which causes it to work. A different kind of scattering effect, I guess.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
It seems that the opal has better performance because it's a volume material, and the scattering effect is compounded many times as the light passes through the thickness of the opal. With etched glass, the scattering effect is produced from essentially a "single" irregular surface.

As a test, I airbrushed multiple layers of a matte varnish on the back surface of a ball lens, while the front surface remained uncoated. When this was inserted into the laser beam, the results were very good. The beam is first diffused through a "volume" diffusion coating, enters and exits the ball lens, is focused, then spreads out again. As the number of airbrushed layers of matte varnish was increased, the speckle was reduced. There is still speckle, but when the ball lens is very close to the plate, say 3 inches, the speckle is rather slight. If a surface is further away, say 4 inches, the speckle is more noticeable. Light transmission is about 45% and quite a bit of polarization is maintained (the green laser pointer I was using was not fully polarized to begin with, so it was difficult to judge).

I think this method has a lot of promise for very up-close reference beams, which would enable a very compact display for holograms. But more development work is needed regarding the volume diffusion coating on the back of the ball lens. Particularly, what kind of material will produce the best kind of scattering effect, what the thickness should be, and how much light it will transmit. I didn't keep track of the number of airbrushed coatings I used, but it may he been around 30 light coatings.

I don't know what material was used in the matte varnish. It wasn't the opaque pigment titanium dioxide, although this is the most common white pigment, and produces a very high level of scatter. TO2 may be an option, if used in very small quantities, although it's well-known for its opacity. A more transparent white pigment is barium sulfate, which may be a good candidate.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Joe Farina:** I would like to pose a question concerning reference beams. I guess the standard reference beam in holography is from a spatial filter, but I've often wondered how much spatial coherence is needed.Say for example, we bounce a laser beam off an aspirin tablet. The beam will be about 2mm in diameter, and the resulting reflected beam will be highly diverging. I tried this, and the spread beam is quite clean. Due the high divergence of the beam, the aspirin tablet will be quite close to the hologram, say 10cm (4 inches). I am wondering if this will work for a reference beam.

The "cleanliness" of a beam has no bearing on the spatial coherence of a beam. The spatial coherence of a beam depends on the source size of the beam. Ed is correct when he says that you can model the spatial coherence of a beam as the individual rays from the source each creating their own set of fringes, slightly displaced as a result of the small angular deviation of the ray direction over the surface are of the source. However since you're recording wavefunctions, to get an exact measure of the spatial coherence of the wavefunction of the beam from the source geometry, you need Van Cittert Zernike theorem, which basically gives the spatial coherence of the source as a function of the fourier transform of the source. In the case of your aspirin, the source size is fairly large because the aspirin scatters, so being a new source derived from the laser. This will result in a fuzzy image. The polished opal may show more promise.

In regards of the image you want to create, this might interest you. The light is an led approximately an inch and a half from the base of the hologram. The image is a Medal of Honor standing about two inch from the plate, ie the image plane is two inches in front. This was an award for a Medal of Honor recipient who was being honored at a dinner at the Navy Medical Center in San Diego.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
With regards to the question of the size of the point-size (spatial coherence) of the reference beam during recording. Wouldn't it be identical to the same requirements as during reconstruction? (For the following, I'm thinking of a simple Denisyuk hologram.)

For reconstruction, say we have a 2mm spot size, spreading out to cover the hologram at a distance of 4 inches. The reconstruction is good and sharp with these parameters (the recording was done with a spatial filter for the reference beam). But say we now consider a non-spatial filter arrangement during recording. Instead of a spatial filter, we use something which passes through a 2mm aperture, but is diffuse within the 2mm aperture (and then spreads out to cover the hologram) Wouldn't the blurriness (or lack thereof) be about the same in both the above examples? Since the first reconstruction was OK with a 2mm diffuse spot, wouldn't this suggest that a *recording* with a 2mm diffuse spot would also be OK, since we are dealing with the same thing (i.e., fringes) during both recording and reconstruction? That is to say, the fringe structure will tolerate a 2mm diffuse spot at that distance, for a sharp reconstruction.

This is just an intuitive guess.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: I don't think so Joe. Recording a diffuse object with a point reference source means recording a unique fringe pattern for every point on the object surface. Recording with a diffuse reference source means recording a unique fringe pattern of each point on the object surface as above for each point in the reference aperture. There's also going to be interference patterns recorded by each point in the reference aperture with all other points in it. That's waaaaaaaaay more information than practical materials can record. Those unrecorded patterns will degrade the object recording.

If an aperture of 1.5mm is placed at the output of the ball lens, enough clean light does get through. If the aperture is reduced to 1mm, the speckle is too noticeable and the output is much reduced.

I've attached a photo with the approximate geometry, with a mock-up of a model, and the spatial filter with a 60x objective. The image area (front of mock-up) is about 2 X 3 inches. The front of the spatial filter is about 3 inches from the center of the image area. The plane of the image area is tilted up 33 degrees from the horizontal (as shown in the photo).
